scope: Documented Odia festival naming, calendar distinctions and textile attribution; no claims of statewide decline or borrowing prevalence.

findings.claim: Official district writing uses Puja (ପୂଜା), Durga Puja (ଦୁର୍ଗାପୂଜା) and Dasahara (ଦଶହରା). These are evidence-backed names to make visible in Odia event descriptions.

sources.locator: Dalkhai section, extracted line37: ଦଶହରା; Bhaijiuntia section, line77: ଦୁର୍ଗାପୂଜା; Pua Jiuntia section, line80: ପୂଜା
Main text paragraphs1–2, extracted lines164–165: ଦଶହରା, ଗଣେଶ ପୂଜା, କାଳୀପୂଜା

findings.limits: Contemporary official attestation, not first recorded usage, historical chronology, pronunciation survey, or evidence that Pujo is wrong in Bengali. Source pages have typographic inconsistencies; quote exact forms only when inspected.

findings.claim: Navratri names nine nights; Dashera/Vijayadashami is the tenth day. They are related observances rather than interchangeable regional names for one duration.

sources.locator: At a glance, extracted lines101 and108

findings.limits: Do not present Maha Dasami as a universal Odia replacement for Navratri. Do not infer Odisha practice from Gujarat-specific vehicle worship, foods or dance descriptions. Avoid tourism page superlatives and antiquity claims.

findings.claim: Sambalpur district places Bhaijiuntia on Mahashtami during Durga Puja and describes Dalkhai in connection with Dasahara and Bhaijiuntia. Local names can introduce readers to an actual practice and its community context.

sources.locator: Dalkhai section lines35–37; Bhaijiuntia section lines75–77

findings.limits: Use situated western Odisha context; do not turn promotional words such as only or all into verified geographic exclusivity or universal participation. Do not flatten local and community distinctions into one statewide ritual.

findings.claim: Odisha’s handloom department identifies Nuapatna with silk Khandua, Sonepur–Boudh with silk Bomkai and tie-dye textiles, Kotpad with vegetable-dyed sarees and scarves, and Kalahandi with Habaspuri. Naming the weave, process and maker gives cultural celebration useful substance.

sources.publisher: Handlooms, Textiles & Handicrafts Department, Government of Odisha
sources.locator: Important Handloom Centers table, lines21–31; especially24–27 and30

findings.limits: This evidence supports positive textile identification, not exclusive ownership of white-and-red colours. Do not classify a wearer or sari solely by colour or treat clothing choice as a test of identity. Regional association, GI status and exclusive colour ownership are different claims.

editorial_recommendation: Use a small contextual naming guide, not a wrong/right table that equates distinct observances. Lead with what readers can name, learn, commission and practise. Mark the explanation of transmission and participation as the article’s argument unless backed by measured evidence.
interpretation: Practical activities are editorial proposals. No measured statewide dilution, causation by cinema, original transcript, local interview or human specialist review claimed.
